facts.text: The double-barred finch lives in dry savannah, grassland and shrubland across northern and eastern Australia.
facts.quote: an estrildid finch found in dry savannah, tropical (lowland) dry grassland and shrubland habitats in northern and eastern Australia

facts.text: It is also called the owl finch because of the dark ring of feathers around its face.
facts.quote: It is sometimes referred to as Bicheno's finch or as the owl finch, the latter of which owing to the dark ring of feathers around the face

facts.text: This little finch has a white face bordered with black, brown upperparts and white underparts.
facts.quote: It has a white face bordered with black, brown upperparts and throat, and white underparts

facts.text: Nests are built in grass, bushes or low trees, with four to six eggs per clutch.
facts.quote: Nests are built in grass, bushes or low trees, with four to six eggs laid per clutch

facts.text: Its call is a soft tet or a louder peew, and its song is a soft fluting like the zebra finch's.
facts.quote: The call is a soft tet or a louder peew, and the song is a soft fluting, which is somewhat like the zebra finch

facts.text: The scientific name bichenovii honours James Ebenezer Bicheno, a colonial secretary of Van Diemen's Land.
facts.quote: The specific epithet commemorates James Ebenezer Bicheno, a colonial secretary of Van Diemen's Land appointed in September 1842

facts.text: The genus name Stizoptera combines Ancient Greek words meaning "to tattoo" and "wing".
facts.quote: The genus name combines the Ancient Greek stizō meaning "to tattoo" with pteron meaning "wing"

facts.text: A neat black line separates the finch's white throat from its white underparts.
facts.quote: The throat and underparts are separated by another black line.

facts.text: The double-barred finch's wings are strikingly patterned in brown and white.
facts.quote: The wings are patterned in brown and white.

facts.text: The double-barred finch was formally described in 1827 by Nicholas Vigors and Thomas Horsfield from Queensland specimens.
facts.quote: The double-barred finch was formally described in 1827 by the naturalists Nicholas Vigors and Thomas Horsfield from specimens collected near Shoalwater Bay and Broad Sound in Queensland, Australia.
